claims.text: Reliable formation of noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanomaterials is governed by achieving atomic-scale homogeneity during synthesis.
Atomic-scale homogeneity governs the catalytic performance of noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanomaterials.
Optimizing synthesis temperature and annealing time promotes rapid, uniform atomic mixing and minimizes local elemental segregation.
Uniformly mixed nanoalloys have enhanced catalytic activity because uniformly distributed active sites exhibit synergistic interactions.
A rapid, well-tuned thermal annealing process can promote uniform atomic diffusion without inducing phase segregation.
There is a thermal-processing window in which atomic mobility overcomes kinetic barriers while extensive grain growth and elemental segregation remain limited.
Excessive annealing time can permit phase separation rather than maximizing atomic mixing.
High-resolution electron microscopy and elemental mapping can measure the degree of atomic-scale homogeneity in these nanoalloys.
Optimized thermal processing causes efficient atomic interdiffusion.
Efficient atomic interdiffusion yields a single-phase, disordered solid solution.
Atomic-scale uniformity prevents the formation of separate phases.
Separate phases reduce the number and synergistic quality of catalytically active sites.
A homogeneous elemental distribution increases the probability of forming favorable multi-element active-site ensembles.
Favorable multi-element active-site ensembles are essential for the catalytic reactions under consideration.
Optimally annealed samples will have a higher density of uniformly distributed active sites than samples receiving standard thermal treatment.
Optimally annealed samples will exhibit higher turnover frequency or selectivity than baseline samples.
Standard thermal treatments sometimes produce partial phase segregation or clustering of noble metals.
The proposed relationship is most likely to hold when the constituent elements have relatively similar atomic radii and bond enthalpies.
The proposed relationship may fail for systems with drastic elemental size mismatches.
The proposed relationship may not extend to bulk materials because their diffusion kinetics differ substantially from those of nanoscale materials.
